title: The Mystery of the Disappearing Mountain
content: Every day, trucks collect tonnes of waste from our homes. But where does it all go? Imagine a mountain of garbage growing every single day outside your city. One day, the mountain just... disappears! How is this possible?

title: What do you think?
content: If we keep throwing things away, why isn't our whole city covered in garbage? Where does the 'away' actually go?

content.title: The Journey of Waste
content.description: Watch how Safai Karamcharis collect garbage and take it to low-lying open areas called Landfills.

title: Landfills
content: The part of the garbage that cannot be reused is separated out and spread over a low-lying open area called a landfill. Once full, it is often converted into a park!

question: What is a low-lying open area where solid waste is dumped called?

title: Think and Reflect
content: What would happen if the landfill near your city became completely full today? Where would tomorrow's garbage go?

title: Connecting the Dots
content: Landfills connect to our geography and environment. A poorly managed landfill can leak harmful chemicals into the groundwater, affecting the water we drink!

title: Waste Audit Mini-Challenge
content: For one day, count how many plastic wrappers you throw away. Can you think of one item you could have reused instead of throwing it in the dustbin?

title: The Magic Soil Recipe
content: Farmers call it 'Black Gold'. It looks like dark soil, smells like earth after rain, and makes plants grow incredibly fast. But it's made entirely out of... dead leaves and leftover food!

title: Socratic Question
content: If you leave a plastic bag and an apple core in the soil for a month, what will happen to them? Will they look the same?

content.title: The Rotting Process
content.description: Watch how microorganisms break down plant and animal waste into manure over time.

title: Composting & Vermicomposting
content: Rotting and conversion of some materials into manure is called 'composting'. When we use Redworms to speed up this process, it's called 'vermicomposting'.

question: Which type of earthworm is used for vermicomposting?

title: Reflect
content: Imagine you are explaining vermicomposting to your younger sibling. How would you explain why we need worms to eat our garbage?

title: The Circle of Life
content: Vermicomposting connects directly to the food chain! Plants take nutrients from the soil, we eat the plants, and our waste goes back to feed the soil.

title: Build a Mini Compost Pit
content: Take a small pot, add some soil, put vegetable peels (no plastic!), and cover it with a little more soil and water. Observe it after two weeks!

title: The Indestructible Material
content: Imagine a material so strong it lasts for 500 years, so light it floats on water, and so cheap it's everywhere. It sounds like a superpower, right? But what happens when we don't want it anymore?

title: What do you think?
content: Look around your room. Count how many things are made of plastic. If plastic never rots, where are the plastic toys your grandparents played with?

content.title: The Plastic Problem
content.description: Visualizing how plastic waste accumulates in oceans and harms marine life.

title: The Curse of Plastics
content: Plastics do not rot or decompose. When burned, they give off harmful gases. When thrown in drains, they cause floods. They are useful, but throwing them away carelessly is a disaster.
Remind students that all plastics are not the same, but all of them take hundreds of years to degrade.
Students often think burning plastic is a good way to get rid of it. Emphasize that burning releases highly toxic gases that cause cancer!

question: Which of the following materials is non-biodegradable?

title: Reflect on Action
content: Think about the last time you used a single-use plastic bag. Could you have carried those items in your hands or a cloth bag instead?

title: Global Impact
content: Plastic waste connects local actions to global problems. A plastic wrapper thrown in a river in India can eventually reach the ocean and harm a turtle miles away.

title: The Plastic-Free Pledge
content: Identify one single-use plastic item in your house (like a straw or a polythene bag) and replace it with a sustainable alternative for one week.
